newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia slashes jobs to boost defence power.
newsitem.headline: Australia slashes jobs to boost defence power.

text.p: Australia announced on Friday that it would slash 8,000 desk jobs from its defence force as part of sweeping reforms to boost front-line operations.
"We're going to shift expenditure from the bureaucracy of defence into the front line of defence," Prime Minister John Howard said.
"There'll be more money to spend on equipment and on the sharp end, the front end. So it's fewer bureaucrats and more soldiers," said Howard.

Defence Minister Ian McLachlan said about 8,000 support jobs would go as part of defence review aimed at shifting 10 percent of the defence budget away from bureaucratic support services and into weapons and training.

The Australian Defence Force has about 57,000 active personnel and some 49,000 reserves. About A$6 billion (US$4.7 billion) of the A$10 billion defence budget goes to the Navy, Army and Air Force, the remainder is spent on administration.
McLachlan said the Australian defence force had to become more efficient as defence spending in the post Cold War world was falling.
Australia's defence spending had fallen from 2.6 percent of gross domestic product 10 years ago to 1.8 percent now.

Author of the defence review, Malcolm McIntosh, a former British defence procurement chief, said Australia also needed to strengthen its defence front line as economically booming Asian nations boosted their military strength.
"Not that long ago, we were a mini-superpower in our own region," McIntosh told reporters on Friday.
"Our economy was substantially larger and the amount we bought for our defence dollar was substantially larger than anyone else around our region," he said.

"That's changing and changing very quickly...the economies around region are growing rapidly and all of those countries are now in a position to acquire the sort of things that only we could afford a few years ago."
